title: Turning points
goals: Combine past and present with mixed conditionals to explain how a decision shapes current life.
Use inverted conditionals (Had I known…, Should you need…, Were it not for…) in formal register.
Express wishes and regrets with wish and if only, and distinguish wish from hope.
Talk about preferences, urgency and advice with would rather, it's (high) time and had better.
Expand vocabulary about decisions, regret and life changes (hindsight, crossroads, bite the bullet).
Reflect on and give advice about decisions with nuance, caution and a natural C1-level register.

learn.title: Mixed conditionals
learn.html:
The type 3 conditional looks at an unreal past with its past consequence (If I had left, I would have missed it). A mixed conditional combines type 3 and type 2 when the tense of the condition and that of the consequence do not match. They are the natural structure for talking about how a past decision shapes the present, or how a lasting trait explains a past event.

TypeCondition (if)ConsequenceExample
Past → presentIf + past perfectwould/could/might + baseIf I had accepted that offer, I would be living in Berlin now.
Present → pastIf + past simple (were)would/could/might + have + past participleIf she weren't so cautious, she would have applied last year.

Points that make the difference:

  • Time markers. They often appear as now, today, still, these days (present result) or at the time, back then, last year (past consequence). They help the reader see the mismatch.
  • Continuity. With a present result, the continuous or stative form is often used: I would be sitting in an office now, we'd still be friends.
  • Degree of certainty. would = an almost certain result; could = possibility or ability; might = uncertainty: If I had studied law, I might be a judge by now.
  • Were / was. In careful register were is kept for all persons (If I were more patient); was appears in informal speech with I/he/she/it.
  • No would in the if-clause. You do not say If I would have known (a very common error, even among native speakers in speech). With would in the if-clause there is only a polite request or willingness (If you would help me, I'd be grateful).
  • Differences in meaning. Compare If I had taken the job, I would be rich (result today) with If I had taken the job, I would have been rich (I would have been rich at that time): the second says nothing about today.

Spanish vs. English: in Spanish the pluperfect subjunctive («si hubiera aceptado») is followed by a simple conditional («viviría») without any problem; the challenge in English is to choose the right verb form in each half, not to translate word by word.

watch.wrong: If I would have studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.
watch.right: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.
watch.why: The if-clause does not take would: use past perfect.

watch.wrong: If I had studied medicine, I would have been a doctor now.
watch.right: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.
watch.why: With now the result is present: would + base, not would have + past participle.

watch.right: If she weren't so cautious, she would have applied.
watch.why: A hypothetical present trait: past simple/were, not present simple.

watch.right: If I hadn't met her, I wouldn't be living here now.
watch.why: The conditioning fact is in the past: past perfect.

learn.title: Inverted conditionals: Had I known…, Should you need…, Were I to…
learn.html:
In formal or literary register you can omit if and invert the subject and the auxiliary. The effect is more elegant and concise, typical of professional writing, public speaking and journalistic style. There are only three patterns, one for each type of condition:

TypeWith ifInverted
Type 3 (unreal past)If I had known, I would have called.Had I known, I would have called.
Type 2 (unreal present/future)If I were you, I would wait. / If I were to win…Were I you, I would wait. / Were I to win…
Possible or polite futureIf you should need help, call me.Should you need help, call me.

Rules and nuances:

  • Negation. Negate with not after the subject and without contracting the auxiliary: Had I not read the small print, I would have signed (never Hadn't I read).
  • Should introduces an unlikely case or a formal instruction: Should you require further assistance, please contact us. The main verb takes the base form.
  • Were to adds a hypothetical or distant nuance: Were the company to relocate, many employees would resign. It equals If the company were to relocate… and is more tentative than if the company relocated.
  • Had it not been for / Were it not for (if it had not been for): Had it not been for her advice, I would never have applied. More neutral synonyms: But for and Without + noun.
  • When not to use it. In casual conversation it sounds affected or distant; it is normal in letters, reports, speeches and writing exams.
  • Combination with mixed conditionals. Had I accepted the offer, I would be a manager now (inversion + mixed): perfectly valid.

Spanish vs. English: Spanish does something similar with «de haber sabido…» and «de ser tú…»; the difference is that English requires the auxiliary (had, were, should) before the subject, and that inversion is obligatory.

watch.wrong: Hadn't I read the small print, I would have signed.
watch.right: Had I not read the small print, I would have signed.
watch.why: In inversion there is no contraction: Had + subject + not.

watch.wrong: Should you will need help, call me.
watch.right: Should you need help, call me.
watch.why: After Should + subject comes the base form, without will.

watch.wrong: Had I would known, I would have called.
watch.right: Had I known, I would have called.
watch.why: Had + subject + past participle; do not add would in the condition.

watch.wrong: Were I know the answer, I would tell you.
watch.right: Were I to know the answer, I would tell you. / If I knew the answer, I would tell you.
watch.why: With Were + subject you use to + infinitive (except with the verb be: Were I you…).

learn.title: wish / if only: regret and wishes
learn.html:
Wish and if only express that reality does not match what we would like. The verb form that follows steps back one stage in time, just as in unreal conditionals. If only is more emphatic and emotional than wish.

Refers to…FormExample
Present (what is not so now)wish + past simple (were)I wish I had more time. / If only I were braver.
Past (regret)wish + past perfectI wish I had listened to my father. / If only I hadn't said that.
Future / someone else's annoying habitwish + would + baseI wish you wouldn't leave your shoes there.
Abilitywish + could (could have + past participle)I wish I could help. / I wish I could have gone.

Key nuances:

  • Wish + would expresses irritation or a wish for change in someone's behaviour, so it is not used with the same subject: one says I wish I could stop, not I wish I would stop. Nor with inanimate things that have no will: I wish it would stop raining is acceptable as a complaint, but I wish the sun would be hotter is not.
  • Wish vs. hope. Hope concerns something that may happen (I hope she calls); wish concerns something unreal or unlikely. With hope the verb tense does not step back.
  • If only takes the same forms: If only I'd known! / If only he would listen! It usually goes with an exclamation or a dramatic pause.
  • Wish + object + to + infinitive is formal and different: I wish to speak to the manager (= I would like to).
  • Would rather. If the wish is a preference rather than a lament, use would rather (see the next block).

For the TOEFL and writing: in formal texts, I regret not having… or It is regrettable that… sounds more sober than I wish I had….

watch.wrong: I wish I would have more patience.
watch.right: I wish I had more patience.
watch.why: Wish about a present state: wish + past simple; would is not used with the same subject.

watch.wrong: I wish I would have listened to my father.
watch.right: I wish I had listened to my father.
watch.why: Past regret: wish + past perfect, not would have.

watch.wrong: If only I would know then what I know now.
watch.right: If only I had known then what I know now.

watch.wrong: I wish I will pass the exam.
watch.right: I hope I pass the exam. / I hope I will pass the exam.
watch.why: Wish is not used with will; for something possible, use hope.

learn.title: would rather, it's (high) time, had better
learn.html:
Three structures for preferences, urgency and advice share one feature: when the subject of the second clause is another person, the verb goes into the past, but the meaning is present or future.

StructurePatternExample
would rather (same subject)would rather + baseI'd rather stay at home tonight.
would rather (other subject, now/future)would rather + subject + past simpleI'd rather you didn't tell anyone.
would rather (other subject, past)would rather + subject + past perfectI'd rather you hadn't mentioned it.
it's (high) timeit's time + subject + past simpleIt's high time we made a decision.
had betterhad better (not) + baseYou'd better check the contract.

Important points:

  • Would rather… than. For comparison: I'd rather resign than work for him (base form on both sides, without to). With prefer one uses to or rather than: I prefer walking to driving.
  • Would rather not is a polite way to decline: Would you like to join us? — I'd rather not, thanks.
  • It's time + to-infinitive vs. + subject + past. It's time to go (general) versus It's time you went (implies that we are already late); high time stresses the reproach.
  • Had better expresses advice with an implicit warning (or there will be consequences); it does not refer to the past despite had. In speech it reduces to 'd better. Negative: You'd better not be late.
  • Would sooner is a literary synonym of would rather: I'd sooner walk than wait.
  • Register. I would rather you did not is a formal, polite request; I'd rather you didn't is the conversational version.

watch.wrong: I'd rather to stay at home.
watch.why: After would rather comes the base form, without to.

watch.wrong: It's time you to start looking for a new flat.
watch.right: It's time you started looking for a new flat.
watch.why: It's time + subject + past simple (present meaning).

watch.wrong: I'd rather you don't tell anyone.
watch.right: I'd rather you didn't tell anyone.
watch.why: With another subject, would rather requires past simple.

watch.wrong: You had better to check the contract.
watch.right: You had better check the contract.

learn.title: Talking about decisions, regrets and alternatives
learn.html:
• Looking back, I think… / With hindsight,… — assess a past decision.
  • If I had it to do over again,… — «if I could do it all again…».
  • I should have + past participle / I shouldn't have + past participle — criticisms of oneself (softer than I wish I had).
  • What if…? / Suppose… — raise alternatives: What if I had stayed?
  • On the one hand… on the other (hand)… — contrast options.
  • It could have been worse. / It's no use crying over spilt milk. — put a mistake into perspective.
  • I can't help wondering whether… — admit persistent doubts.
  • All things considered, I'd still… / I'd do it again. — close with an evaluation.
  • The die is cast. — the decision has been made and cannot be undone.

write.prompt: Write a reflection of 270 to 330 words about a turning point in your life (a decision you made or avoided). Say what happened, what your life would be like if you had decided otherwise, and what you have learnt. Use at least one mixed conditional, one inverted conditional (Had I…), an expression with wish or if only, and vocabulary such as crossroads, hindsight, trade-off or leap of faith.
checklist: A mixed conditional with the correct tense shift
An inverted conditional without contraction (Had I not…)
At least one sentence with wish or if only
Three decision vocabulary words used accurately
A reflective tone with nuance (admittedly, in hindsight)
Organised paragraphs: context, decision, consequences, learning
Between 270 and 330 words
write.model:
At twenty-eight, I found myself at a crossroads. A software company in Toronto offered me a position with a generous salary, and all I had to do was say yes. Instead, I turned it down. My mother had recently been ill, my relationship was still fragile, and the idea of leaving everything behind felt like too great a leap of faith. I told myself that the decision was purely rational although, admittedly, fear played a larger part than I was willing to acknowledge.

In hindsight, it was a decision with real trade-offs. If I had accepted the offer, I would be living in a very different city now, probably earning twice as much and speaking with a slightly different accent. I might not have my current job, which I love, and I would almost certainly not be sharing a flat with the person I married three years later. Had I not stayed, I would never have met her at a friend's wedding, a thought that still unsettles me.

Even so, I sometimes wish I had been braver. I wish I had at least gone for six months, and if only I had asked myself what I wanted rather than what I feared losing. Careers can be rebuilt, but chances to live abroad are less common than we imagine, and I have never entirely shaken the feeling of a door left closed.

What have I learnt? Mainly that no decision is purely rational, and that regret, in moderation, is a useful teacher. Had I been given the chance again, I might well have chosen differently, yet I doubt I would have been happier. Perhaps the real lesson is that a good life can be built on either side of a crossroads, provided we commit fully to the path we take.

write.prompt: A friend is torn between keeping a stable job and leaving it to start a project of their own. Write them an advice letter of 260 to 320 words. End with your recommendation and a warm but honest tone.

At least one inversion with Should or Had

I'd rather you + past simple or past perfect
Vocabulary: comfort zone, setback, fall back on, take the plunge
Contrast linkers (on the other hand, that said)
Between 260 and 320 words
write.model:
Dear Carlos,

I was glad to hear from you, although I could tell from your message how torn you feel. Let me try to help you think it through, as someone who has been there.

On the one hand, your current job offers security, a decent salary and colleagues you like. On the other, you have told me for two years that you feel stuck, and that is not something to ignore. It's high time you decided whether staying is a choice or just a habit. Frankly, I'd rather you made the decision deliberately than drifted into it.

Let me tell you about my cousin Laia. She left a stable post at a bank to open a small bakery. The first year was hard: she had to fall back on her savings, and she suffered a major setback when her oven broke down in December. Yet she never regretted taking the plunge, because she had prepared. Before leaving, she had saved eight months of expenses and tested her recipes at weekend markets. Had she gone in blindly, she would probably have failed.

That, I think, is the point. You had better not resign until you have a financial cushion and some evidence that people will pay for your idea. Should you find that the demand is real, the risk will look much smaller. Should it not, you will have lost little, and you will still have your job. Leaving your comfort zone need not mean burning your bridges: could you start the project in the evenings first?

That said, I'd rather you didn't wait for perfect conditions, because they rarely come. If I were you, I would set a deadline of six months and then decide.

Whatever you choose, I'll support you. Just be honest with yourself about what you really want.

With love,

Marta

reading.title: The road not taken, and the one I took
reading.intro: Read this personal essay about a decision and its consequences, then answer the questions.
paragraphs: Everyone has a version of the same story. Somewhere in the past there is a Tuesday afternoon, an unremarkable room, a document waiting for a signature, and a decision that felt small at the time. Only years later, with the benefit of hindsight, do we recognise it as a crossroads. If I had not answered that email in the spring of 2016, I would still be running quarterly reports for a logistics firm in Monterrey. Instead, I am writing this from a rented attic in Oaxaca, with a half-finished manuscript and an uncertain income.

The email was an invitation to apply for a three-month fellowship at a small publishing house. I almost ignored it. My salary was good, my manager liked me, and I had just taken out a mortgage. Had I sat down and weighed up every pros-and-cons list I had ever drawn, the sensible column would have won by a mile. What tipped the balance was not courage; it was a gut feeling I could not justify to anyone, least of all to my mother, who asked, quite reasonably, whether I had lost my mind.

Psychologists who study regret have long observed an asymmetry. In the short run, people tend to feel worse about actions that went wrong than about opportunities they let pass. Over decades, the pattern reverses: it is the road not taken that haunts us. I am cautious about generalising from a handful of studies, and I know that regret is also shaped by temperament; some people are simply more prone to brooding than others. Still, the idea rings true. The people I interviewed for this piece rarely said, 'I wish I hadn't tried.' They said, 'I wish I had tried sooner.'

Take Marta, a civil engineer who retrained as a pastry chef at forty-one. She describes the first year as the hardest of her life. 'I would rather have kept my pension,' she admitted, laughing, 'but I'd rather not have kept it at the price of my curiosity.' Or Joaquín, who turned down a transfer to Chicago and still wonders, a decade later, what his life would be like if he had gone. He is not unhappy; he just cannot stop running the alternative film in his head. 'Should I ever get a second chance,' he told me, 'I would take the plunge without thinking twice.'

What these stories share is not a moral, however tempting one might be. Leaping is not always wise. Some leaps end badly, and anyone who tells you otherwise is selling a book, preferably their own. My fellowship led to nothing for eight months, and I came close, more than once, to cutting my losses and crawling back to my old desk. It was a modest commission, almost an afterthought, that kept me going. Without it, I would probably have given up.

If there is a lesson, it is a modest one. Decisions are rarely as binary as we imagine; most of them can be tested, staged or reversed at some cost. The real discipline lies in telling apart the choices that are genuinely irreversible from those that merely feel that way. And once the choice is made, it is worth resisting the urge to rewrite it. It is time we stopped treating hindsight as wisdom: it is merely information we did not have when it mattered. I do sometimes wish I had saved more money, and I wish my mother had been less right about the winter heating bills. But I have never wished I had stayed.

listening.title: Second Thoughts: a radio call-in
listening.intro: Listen to a radio programme in which a caller asks for advice about a decision. You can play it again.

lines.text: Welcome back to Second Thoughts. Our next caller is Elena, who says she's at a crossroads. Elena, what's going on?
Hi. Well, I've been offered a job in Vancouver, and I can't decide whether to take it. I'm honestly in two minds.
Mostly my parents. If I moved, I wouldn't see them for months at a time. I wish I could split myself in two.
That's a common dilemma. Let me ask you this. Had you been offered the job ten years ago, would you have hesitated?
Honestly, no. I'd have been on the next plane. But I'd rather not repeat my brother's mistake. He moved abroad and regrets it.
Interesting. So are you afraid of regretting the move, or of regretting staying?
Both, I suppose. It's high time I made a decision, but every time I do, I have second thoughts.
Let's bring in our guest, Dr. Ruiz, a psychologist who has written about regret.
Thanks. Elena, one thing I'd suggest is to separate what is reversible from what isn't. Should you take the job and hate it, you could come back. A year abroad isn't a life sentence.
That's true. I hadn't thought of it as a trial.
Exactly. And if you stay, ask yourself what you'd be doing in five years that you wouldn't be doing if you'd gone. If the answer excites you, that's a sign.
Elena, we'll have to leave it there. Any final thoughts?
Just that I'd rather decide with a clear head than wait until someone decides for me. Thank you both.
